title: Media Blitz

jokes.text: Ron finds a typewriter next to the dumpster and lovingly describes it like a prized antique: 'An old Underwood 5 with original carriage return. Took her home, polished her up and bought a brand new ribbon off of electronicbay.com.'
jokes.setup: Ron describes the typewriter with reverent, almost romantic detail, as if it were a magnificent find.
jokes.punchline: 'electronicbay.com' — Ron's obliviousness to eBay's actual name caps his luddite persona perfectly.
jokes.explanation: The joke is elegant in how it encapsulates Ron's entire worldview: he finds something discarded and restores it with pride, then buys supplies from a website he doesn't even know the real name of. 'electronicbay.com' is a perfect character detail — specific, surprising, and could only come from this character. High character integration score because this joke is meaningless without knowing Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I found something special. Something truly remarkable. This is the kind of discovery that changes a man's life.

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: Ron, that's a broken desk lamp from a dumpster.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A broken desk lamp from a dumpster that somebody didn't want anymore. Do you know what that means? It means it's free. And anything free is worth ten times what you paid for it.

jokes.text: Ron's threat note: 'If you sons of bitches try to remove this typewriter, I'll kill you.' Then: 'I'm going to type every word I know! Rectangle. America.'
jokes.setup: Colleagues wonder what Ron is typing on his newly acquired typewriter.
jokes.punchline: His note is a death threat, followed by the reveal that he's now just typing random words like 'Rectangle. America.' — equal parts menacing and absurd.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's standout moments. The escalation from menacing death threat to childlike 'Rectangle. America.' is perfectly structured — it's both completely absurd and completely in character. Ron threatening coworkers is expected; Ron sitting there typing 'Butthole' with the same gravitas is unexpected and hilarious. The economy is outstanding: three words deliver maximum comedy. 'Rectangle. America. Megaphone. Monday. Butthole.' is a legendary Ron Swanson bit that's endlessly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I found a 1952 Hermes 3000 typewriter on electronicbay.com for a reasonable price.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, it's eBay. E-B-A-Y.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's what I said. Electronicbay.com.

jokes.text: Ben declares 'I'm going to type every word I know!' and then types: 'Rectangle. America. Megaphone. Monday. Butthole.'
jokes.setup: Ben's unhinged threat has been read aloud; he doubles down with a new, equally bizarre declaration
jokes.punchline: His word list escalates through perfectly random nouns and concludes with 'Butthole' — the comic nadir that makes the absurdity complete
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. The escalating list of random words is carefully curated — 'Rectangle. America. Megaphone. Monday.' all feel plausibly like words someone would type to test a typewriter, making the final 'Butthole' land perfectly as the inevitable comic destination. The structure is immaculate: four straight-faced nouns, then the payoff. The economy is near-perfect. Highly quotable and memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I don't understand why everyone keeps complaining about my typewriter. It's a beautiful machine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ron, you've been typing the same memo for three hours. And it's just the word 'no' repeated 47 times.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Efficient communication.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry Gergich
dialogue.line: My ears are bleeding.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Harris
dialogue.line: That's acute acoustic trauma.

jokes.text: Ben corrects Leslie's '35%' to '34.2%' and Leslie imitates him in a robot voice: 'I'm Ben, the numbers robot.'
jokes.setup: Leslie rounds 34.2% awareness to '35%,' and Ben pedantically corrects her.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's mocking impression — 'I'm Ben, the numbers robot' — immediately characterizes their dynamic.
jokes.explanation: A solid character comedy moment that efficiently establishes Ben's pedantry and Leslie's impatience. The 'numbers robot' line is memorable and fits both characters well. Not groundbreaking but well-executed workplace banter.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm typing threats to protect my typewriter.

jokes.text: Leslie says she called Oprah, then immediately walks it back: 'Well, I tried to call Oprah. I couldn't get her number. I'm putting it out there, like The Secret. And hopefully, she'll call me.'
jokes.setup: Leslie announces impressive-sounding media outreach for Harvest Fest.
jokes.punchline: She couldn't get Oprah's number and is now relying on manifestation philosophy.
jokes.explanation: The Oprah gambit is quintessential Leslie — her overreach is endearing and absurd, and pivoting to 'like The Secret' is a great character-specific justification. The joke lands because it's simultaneously delusional and sincere. Strong character integration because this only works for Leslie.

jokes.text: Ben reacts with visible horror to the radio hosts' names: 'Crazy Ira and... The Douche.' Delivered as a slow, incredulous read.
jokes.setup: Leslie enthusiastically announces their first interview is with 'Crazy Ira and The Douche.'
jokes.punchline: Ben's horrified pause and re-reading of 'The Douche' signals he cannot believe this is a real thing.
jokes.explanation: A clean straight-man reaction beat. Ben's outsider-in-Pawnee perspective is well-utilized, and the deadpan re-read of 'The Douche' is a reliable comedy tool. Functional and charming but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Leslie defends Crazy Ira and The Douche: 'So much better than Tubby Tony and the Papaya. Am I right? They're seriously so funny.'
jokes.setup: Ben is clearly horrified by the radio hosts' names.
jokes.punchline: Leslie not only defends them but offers an even more absurd alternative — 'Tubby Tony and the Papaya' — as the worse option, proving Pawnee's bar is underground.
jokes.explanation: 'Tubby Tony and the Papaya' is a brilliantly absurd invention. The joke's strength is in its specificity — a lesser writer would've just said 'the other guys are worse,' but naming them something this ridiculous both establishes Pawnee's cultural ecosystem and gets a genuine laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've been compiling a list of words that should be permanently removed from the English language. Words like 'moist,' 'tender,' and 'ponder.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: However, I've decided to add one more word to that list.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And that word is... well, let me just say it involves a four-letter word that rhymes with 'duck,' followed by 'taco.'

jokes.text: April, asked to consider a job in Indianapolis, lists her conditions: 'That sounds boring. But I have nothing keeping me here. Do you have Internet in your office? Yes. Fine, I'll do it.'
jokes.setup: Chris offers April a prestigious job at the state house with relocation benefits.
jokes.punchline: April's entire decision-making process hinges on whether there's Internet, delivered with total deadpan.
jokes.explanation: April's nihilistic decision-making is perfectly captured in this exchange. 'I have nothing keeping me here' followed immediately by 'Do you have Internet?' is a great character beat — her indifference to career ambition contrasted with her one basic requirement. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, it was 47 percent, not 48.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh wow, Ben Wyatt everybody. The man who can tell you the exact percentage of his own irrelevance.

jokes.text: Ann asks what the meeting was about and Andy says: 'It turns out Chris is my real dad.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks Andy what the mysterious meeting between April and Chris was about.
jokes.punchline: Andy's completely fabricated and absurd answer — delivered with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: A quick, efficient Andy joke. His inability to parse reality combined with his total confidence makes this work. 'I think you're lying' from Ann is also a perfect understated response. Short, clean, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm very precise with my words.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, you're very precise with your words? That's great. I'm very precise with my words too. We're both very precise. We're precision guys.

jokes.text: April's confessional about Andy: 'Unless Andy can un-kiss Ann, then I'm not going to change my mind. But if he wants to take my dumb sister to her dumb dance class, then I'm not going to dumb stop him.'
jokes.setup: April explains her stance on Andy's attempts to win her over.
jokes.punchline: The repetition of 'dumb' three times in a row — 'dumb sister,' 'dumb dance class,' 'dumb stop him' — revealing April's emotional investment through childish petulance.
jokes.explanation: The triple 'dumb' is a wonderful April character beat — her attempt to sound cool and indifferent collapses into obvious emotional investment. The grammatically wrong 'dumb stop him' is the funniest part, and it's clearly intentional. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've been manifesting a call from Oprah using The Secret. I made a vision board, I wrote affirmations, I even burned sage in the shape of her face. The universe is listening. Any day now, Oprah's going to call me and we're going to talk about my initiative.

jokes.text: Crazy Ira's radio bit: 'You know why I'd never be an astronaut? Two words. Space farts. You can't roll down the window of the shuttle.'
jokes.setup: Crazy Ira launches into a hacky radio-DJ comedy bit about astronauts.
jokes.punchline: 'Space farts. You can't roll down the window of the shuttle.'
jokes.explanation: The joke is intentionally weak — Crazy Ira is meant to be a mediocre radio DJ, so the hacky material is appropriate in-world. The craft score reflects the intentional badness of the material, which still functions as a joke because the audience understands the meta-commentary. Not remarkable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have two radio hosts here today. First, we have Harris, and then we have... The Douche.

jokes.text: Crazy Ira and The Douche do a Neil Armstrong parody bit, mocking the 'one small step' quote with crude substitutions.
jokes.setup: The radio hosts riff on the space farts bit by bringing in Neil Armstrong's famous quote.
jokes.punchline: Deliberately mangled 'one small step' quote stands in for crude punchline, demonstrating the hosts' low-brow style.
jokes.explanation: Again, intentionally hacky radio-DJ material. The joke about The Douche's name lands in naming alone. The Neil Armstrong riff is meant to show how bad the radio hosts are, which serves the episode's purposes, but it's genuinely weak comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Crazy Ira and The Douche are actually really talented. They're just as good as some of the other radio personalities out there.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I mean, they're no worse than Imus or Stern or any of those guys.

jokes.text: The Douche introduces Tom as 'Tom Haverfart.'
jokes.setup: The Douche reads the guests' names.
jokes.punchline: 'Tom Haverfart' — juvenile name substitution that embarrasses Tom but also reveals The Douche's maturity level.
jokes.explanation: Juvenile potty humor, but effective at establishing The Douche's character and it's the kind of thing that gets a real chuckle in context. Not sophisticated but fits the world-building purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You know, the key to optimal physical fitness is maintaining a consistent regimen with proper form, adequate hydration, and a balanced macronutrient intake. I've been tracking my metrics for seventeen years and—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you say one more thing about your metrics, I'm leaving.

jokes.text: Leslie describes Harvest Festival as 'where fun meets awesome. Meets agriculture.'
jokes.setup: Leslie launches into her enthusiastic Harvest Festival pitch.
jokes.punchline: 'Meets agriculture.' — the completely mundane third entry after two excitement words.
jokes.explanation: The rule of three broken on the third beat is a classic comedy structure, and 'agriculture' is a perfectly deflating word. It's both very Leslie (she genuinely believes agriculture is exciting) and gently absurd. Clean and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: April, I'd like to offer you a position in my office.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: What are the benefits?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, we have a 401k, health insurance, paid time off—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Do you have internet?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yes, of course.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm in.

jokes.text: The Douche says 'You lost your virginity in a corn maze, didn't you, Douche?' — then Crazy Ira confirms 'That's right. To your mom.' Followed by 'Crazy Ira! Clean your room!' from The Douche.
jokes.setup: Leslie mentions the best corn maze ever at Harvest Fest.
jokes.punchline: The 'your mom' joke followed by 'Crazy Ira! Clean your room!' — implying Crazy Ira still lives with his mom, who is apparently present.
jokes.explanation: The 'your mom' joke is cheap, but the callback of Crazy Ira's mom literally calling into the studio to tell him to clean his room elevates it significantly. The layering — Ira makes a crass your-mom joke and his actual mom calls to scold him — is well-structured for a quick bit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What was that meeting about?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Oh, we were just discussing the upcoming town hall and how we need to increase budget allocation for squirrel prevention. Apparently we've had seventeen confirmed squirrel incidents this month alone. It's a real crisis. They're getting bolder.

jokes.text: Leslie adds: 'There's also going to be hay rides,' and The Douche responds: '"Hey, ride me," is what Crazy Ira's mom said.' Tom: 'China Joe, you are a poet.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to pivot to a different festival feature.
jokes.punchline: The Douche does an immediate hay/hey wordplay 'your mom' callback, and Tom's 'China Joe, you are a poet' is a bizarre non-sequitur compliment.
jokes.explanation: The hay/hey pun is serviceable, and Tom inexplicably calling The Douche 'China Joe' is a strange character moment that implies Tom has already given him a nickname, suggesting his eagerness to ingratiate himself. Mildly amusing.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy is dumb. Like, really dumb. He's so dumb that he makes other dumb people feel smart. He's dumb-dumb. And not like a fun dumb, like a dumb dumb. Like a dumb stop.

jokes.text: A man storms the permits desk: 'My bird is missing. I need a permit to post signs.' Andy: 'Let me just look for that form.' Man: 'There's no time! He can fly!'
jokes.setup: Andy is working the permits desk as part of his April-pleasing deal.
jokes.punchline: 'There's no time! He can fly!' — the frantic logic of the bird owner (the bird can fly away, so the situation is urgent), delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'There's no time! He can fly!' is a great bit of absurdist Pawnee citizen comedy. The internal logic is sound (a flying bird is harder to find), but the frantic delivery makes it feel deeply unhinged. The economy is excellent — four words do all the heavy lifting.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: Because in space, no one can hear you fart.

jokes.text: Andy confidently declares: 'I eat "running the permits desk for an hour" for breakfast.' Then immediately hurts himself: 'Ow. That's... Ow.'
jokes.setup: Andy brags about his ability to handle the permits desk.
jokes.punchline: He immediately injures himself doing something routine, undercutting his bravado.
jokes.explanation: The joke structure is textbook: big talk immediately undercut by incompetence. The line 'I eat [X] for breakfast' is a familiar expression, but Andy's immediate self-injury is a well-timed physical beat. High character integration — Andy's confidence-to-incompetence ratio is his defining trait.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: That's one small step for man, one giant... PRRRRIIIIIP for mankind.

jokes.text: Tom asks Andy why he's at the permits desk: 'Why are you working the permits desk, and why was that child clubbing your nuggets?'
jokes.setup: Tom encounters Andy in an unexpected situation.
jokes.punchline: 'Clubbing your nuggets' — Tom's idiosyncratic slang for a child hitting Andy in the groin.
jokes.explanation: 'Clubbing your nuggets' is quintessential Tom Haverford — his tendency to invent absurd slang is a running character trait, and this is a particularly good example. It's specific, unexpected, and could only come from Tom. The question also implies we briefly see the child hitting Andy, which is a bonus visual gag.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: We're changing your name to Haverfart.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? No!

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: Too late, Haverfart. That's your name now.

jokes.text: Ben confessional: 'No, I don't care about their relationship. I just don't want to lose April. I would never be able to find a worse assistant.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains why he's invested in April staying.
jokes.punchline: 'I would never be able to find a worse assistant.' — the reason he wants to keep her is because she's terrible at her job.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured anti-compliment. Ben builds to what sounds like an emotional admission, then the punchline inverts our expectations entirely — he wants to keep the worst employee because she's reliably terrible. The economy is excellent, and the deadpan delivery of this line makes it even better. It also says something true about Ben's character: he's grown fond of chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: So you and your boyfriend—

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Your mom.

jokes.text: Crazy Ira announces he's looking Ben up on 'AltaVista.'
jokes.setup: The radio hosts decide to investigate Ben on-air.
jokes.punchline: They use AltaVista — a long-obsolete search engine — to do it, establishing the show's Pawnee-as-backwater running joke.
jokes.explanation: The AltaVista joke is a solid piece of world-building comedy — Pawnee is technologically and culturally behind. The joke earns a callback later (Ben's excellent 'Is it 1997?' response), which retroactively improves this setup.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Hey, it's Ira's mom. I'm so proud of my son. He's doing so well with his business ventures.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: You know what I love about the fall? Hay rides.

dialogue.speaker: The Douche
dialogue.line: Hey, ride me.

jokes.text: Reaction shot/beat: Ira reveals Ben was elected mayor at 18 and bankrupted a city with an ice skating rink called 'Ice Town.' Ben's visible flop sweat — described by Ira: 'I really wish you guys could see this guy right now. He is drenched in sweat.'
jokes.setup: Ben is pulled into the interview spotlight and his embarrassing past is aired live on radio.
jokes.punchline: Ben's complete meltdown is described in real time by the radio hosts — 'he is drenched in sweat.'
jokes.explanation: The cringe comedy of Ben's public meltdown is the episode's central comedic engine. It's well-constructed: the embarrassment escalates across multiple interviews, and this first instance establishes the pattern. The detail of the sweat being described on radio (because listeners can't see it) is a smart structural choice. High impact because cringe comedy with a beloved character hits hard.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You need a permit to post missing bird signs.

dialogue.speaker: Citizen
dialogue.line: But it's a missing bird. It can fly. By the time I post signs, it'll be in another state.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Then I don't see why you need the signs.

jokes.text: The hosts force Ben to say 'Ice Town.' Long pause. 'Ice Town.'
jokes.setup: The hosts taunt Ben about the name of his failed project.
jokes.punchline: After a painfully long pause, Ben quietly admits 'Ice Town' — the name lands as both silly and devastating.
jokes.explanation: The name 'Ice Town' does enormous comedic work. It's a genuinely funny name for a catastrophically failed project — grandiose dreams embodied in two simple, slightly ridiculous words. The pause before Ben says it, and his defeated 'I was a kid' follow-up, is perfect cringe comedy. 'Ice Town' becomes the episode's defining repeated punchline. Economy score near-perfect because the name itself is the whole joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I eat nails for breakfast.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Without milk?

jokes.text: Camera host notes: 'I really wish you guys could see this guy right now. He is drenched in sweat.' Ben is visibly falling apart on air.
jokes.setup: Ben is having a live breakdown on radio — a medium where the audience can't see him
jokes.punchline: The radio host calls attention to what listeners can't see — Ben's physical deterioration — making it a visual joke described verbally
jokes.explanation: A clever structural joke — the radio host essentially does the camera's job for us. The comedy is that this is both descriptive and cruelly accurate. We know Ben is a sweating disaster, and having it announced on air to all of Pawnee extends the humiliation perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I got this. I'm a professional permit clerk now.

dialogue.speaker: Henry
dialogue.line: Dad, watch this!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ow! Hey, what are you—ow! Not there! Henry, stop!

dialogue.speaker: Henry
dialogue.line: You said you were a professional!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A professional at permits, not at being repeatedly kicked in the groin!

jokes.text: Caller from 'Douche Nation' calls in: 'What's up, guys? Just douching over here in Eagleton.'
jokes.setup: The show takes a caller from listeners.
jokes.punchline: 'Just douching over here in Eagleton' — the caller uses 'douching' as a verb for hanging out, establishing the radio show's absurd fan culture.
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist bit on Pawnee's radio culture. The verbification of 'douching' is mildly amusing and fits the show's world-building. The Eagleton reference adds a layer for regular viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't care about April's relationship. What she does in her personal time is her business.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But if she leaves this department, I will lose the world's worst assistant, and frankly, I've grown accustomed to her face.

jokes.text: Ben's complete verbal collapse in the interview: 'The funny... When... I guess... The fortunate... Can we just, sort of...'
jokes.setup: A caller asks about Ben being elected mayor at a young age.
jokes.punchline: Ben's attempt to form a coherent sentence collapses into fragments — he cannot complete a single thought.
jokes.explanation: The verbal collapse is the comedic peak of the radio interview. 'The funny... When... I guess... The fortunate...' is a masterclass in scripted-improvisation: it sounds genuinely like someone short-circuiting under pressure. The fragments being structured as increasing approximations of coherent thought makes it funnier than a simple 'uhhh.' High impact score because the audience would be losing it.

dialogue.speaker: Crazy Ira
dialogue.line: We did some research on Ben Wyatt using AltaVista.

dialogue.speaker: Roger Refrigerator
dialogue.line: Yeah, we found out he's a nerd.

jokes.text: 'Game over, man. Game over.' The Douche's assessment of Ben's interview.
jokes.setup: Ben's interview collapses into incoherence.
jokes.punchline: The Douche quotes Aliens — 'Game over, man. Game over' — to summarize the disaster.
jokes.explanation: A familiar pop-culture quote used appropriately. Not original but lands because it perfectly captures the moment and is in character for The Douche. The follow-up 'Nice job, man. Was that your first time talking to other people? Because it came off that way' is a sharper follow-up insult.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Host
dialogue.line: Come on, Ben, just tell us the name of the project.

dialogue.speaker: Radio Host
dialogue.line: What was it called?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It was called the Cones of Dunshire.

jokes.text: 'Nice job, man. Was that your first time talking to other people? Because it came off that way.'
jokes.setup: Ben's interview has completely fallen apart.
jokes.punchline: Ira delivers a precisely cruel burn: Ben seemed like he'd never spoken to humans before.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed insult that's specific enough to be memorable. 'Was that your first time talking to other people?' is an unusually precise mockery that earns a laugh both from its accuracy and its brutality.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Get away from her, you bitch!

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional damage control spin: 'You embarrassed me in front of The Douche... No worries. Look, it was just a bump in the road. Okay. Fortunately, the Leslie-mobile is an all-terrain vehicle.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to reassure Ben while simultaneously roasting him.
jokes.punchline: 'Fortunately, the Leslie-mobile is an all-terrain vehicle.' — Leslie's self-aggrandizement as crisis management.
jokes.explanation: 'The Leslie-mobile is an all-terrain vehicle' is perfectly Leslie — she casts herself as a vehicle of relentless optimism, and the metaphor is both grandiose and specific. The fact that she says 'You embarrassed me in front of The Douche' without self-awareness is also a great character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? A calculator wearing sunglasses would be more personable than you right now.

jokes.text: Leslie's confessional: 'So, everything involving Ben is fine. I just need to talk to you in private about something different that is not Ben-related. Ben, good job.'
jokes.setup: Leslie tries to manage the situation while being recorded by documentary cameras.
jokes.punchline: Her attempt to speak 'privately' on camera while Ben is present, concluding with the hollow 'Ben, good job,' is perfectly absurd crisis PR.
jokes.explanation: The meta-comedy of Leslie trying to speak privately while on camera, combined with her obviously false 'Ben, good job,' is sharp situational comedy. It's a mockumentary-specific joke that works because of the format.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So, uh, Pawnee has a lot of... cars. People drive them. On the roads. Which is where cars go.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Some of them are red. Or blue. Or... the other colors that cars can be.

jokes.text: Leslie's assessment of Ben to Tom: 'Well, we should just slap a pair of Ray-Bans on a calculator, because that would be way more charming.'
jokes.setup: Leslie privately tells Tom that Ben is useless for media appearances.
jokes.punchline: 'Slap a pair of Ray-Bans on a calculator' — a vivid, specific image for Ben's robotic charm.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The image of a calculator wearing Ray-Bans is so specific and vivid that it transcends the generic 'he's not charming' observation. It earns its high score because it's both a great callback to the 'numbers robot' characterization AND an original, memorable image that stands on its own. The economy is near-perfect: the visual does all the work. This is the kind of line that makes a writers' room proud.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann, I need to tell you something important. Something I've been holding back.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What is it, Chris?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Your apartment has terrible feng shui. The energy in here is completely blocked. You need to rearrange everything immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's what you were being so mysterious about?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: The chi is stagnant, Ann. Stagnant!

jokes.text: Ben's attempt at small talk with the cameraman after his humiliation: 'So, how are you liking Pawnee? There are a lot of cars. I mean, not too many. Trucks and stuff. But, you know... Cool. Good talk, Ice Town. Okay.'
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to recover from his radio disaster by making normal conversation.
jokes.punchline: His small talk is excruciating — 'There are a lot of cars. I mean, not too many' — and he ends by calling himself 'Ice Town.'
jokes.explanation: 'Good talk, Ice Town' is a delicious self-own — Ben has so thoroughly internalized his humiliation that he refers to himself by the nickname. The small talk preceding it is brilliantly bad: 'There are a lot of cars. I mean, not too many' captures the exact texture of someone whose brain has stopped working. High rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay, you can rearrange my furniture.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Really? This is the best day of my life!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yeah, just... try not to move things too much.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm going to move EVERYTHING.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Your couch is going against that wall!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Sure.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Your bed is going in the living room!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm painting your walls a different color!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Whatever you want.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ann... are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I don't even know who I am anymore.

jokes.text: Chris describes his salad: 'Wow. Who knew that watercress, garbanzo beans and walnuts could complement each other so well? Good dressing, too, right? Flaxseed and agave. Same basic ingredients as bird feed.'
jokes.setup: Chris enthusiastically promotes his healthy salad.
jokes.punchline: 'Same basic ingredients as bird feed' — Chris is eating bird food and considers this a selling point.
jokes.explanation: Chris's wellness obsession is a reliable character comedy vein, and 'bird feed' as a positive comparison is a good reveal. It's not his strongest moment but fits his character well.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Well, I guess you could say this conversation is really... ear-iting. Get it? Corn? Because corn has ears?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: And I'm not trying to be un-beet-able with these puns, but I think I'm really crop-ping up with good material.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: You're not laughing. I guess you could say the vibe is getting a little... stalky. Stalk? Corn stalk?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Lettuce just agree these are gourd puns. Get it? Like the gourds you use in fall decorations?

jokes.text: Chris announces: 'I want to define your bagua.' Ann: 'Okay. What's that?' Chris: 'It's a feng shui term. The energy in this house is a little stale. But I think I can redefine your flow in a very positive way.'
jokes.setup: Chris is supposedly discussing something relationship-related with Ann.
jokes.punchline: He's actually talking about feng shui — 'I want to define your bagua' is his way of saying he wants to rearrange her furniture.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection of 'bagua' sounding like a relationship proposition is moderately effective. Chris's wellness-speak as relationship avoidance is a good character beat, even if the joke itself is somewhat predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're colleagues with benefits.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, we work together and we get health insurance, dental, a 401k...

jokes.text: Ann's confessional about Chris's obliviousness: 'Am I not being obvious enough? I feel like I'm being obvious.'
jokes.setup: Chris has completely pivoted to rearranging furniture instead of addressing their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Ann's camera look / confessional — her exasperation at Chris's cluelessness is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A clean talking-head beat. Ann's frustrated self-questioning is relatable and well-delivered. The economy is strong — two sentences do all the work — but the concept isn't particularly fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dear Mrs. Johnson, thank you for the lovely gift—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's Mr. Johnson. He's a man.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right, right. Dear Mr. Johnson, thank you for the lovely gift. Your generosity means so much to me and my wife.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's not married.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay. Dear Mr. Johnson, thank you for the lovely gift. As a fellow man, I appreciate your manly generosity.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why would you say that?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because he's a man!

jokes.text: Tom's pre-written Harvest Fest plug: 'Harvest Festival more like "Harvest Bestival." The Parks Department has planted the seeds, and now, they're harvesting the rewards. They'll put the fun in funnel cake.' Then: 'Okay. Now, I'm done.'
jokes.setup: Tom is apparently using his newspaper interview to deliver a pre-written publicity blurb.
jokes.punchline: 'Okay. Now, I'm done.' — the blurb is so obviously canned that Tom formally announces its conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Tom's self-awareness about his own PR speak is a decent meta-joke. 'Harvest Bestival' is groan-worthy in the right way, and 'fun in funnel cake' is solid wordplay. The 'Okay. Now, I'm done' punctuation is the best part.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dear Mrs. Henderson, thank you for the lovely gift of the casserole dish.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, it was a serving platter.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, no, a decorative bowl. A decorative bowl shaped like a duck.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The duck is blue. No, green. It's definitely green and it quacks when you press it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Which is weird because I don't think ducks are supposed to quack at that pitch. That's more of a seagull sound.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Anyway, thank you for the rubber seagull. We love it.

jokes.text: Leslie accidentally describes Ben to reporter Shauna Malwae-Tweep: 'And he's easy on the eyes, too.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is doing damage control about Ben for the newspaper.
jokes.punchline: She accidentally reveals her attraction to Ben mid-professional-defense.
jokes.explanation: A clean Leslie slip — her professionalism crumbles around Ben. It's character-consistent and sets up the 'colleagues with benefits' punchline perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Perd, you ever see RoboCop? You're like RoboCop, but instead of being part man, part machine, you're part man, part... news.

dialogue.speaker: Perd
dialogue.line: That's the worst thing anyone's ever said to me.

jokes.text: 'We are colleagues with benefits. We're colleagues who benefit from the fact that we're also friends.'
jokes.setup: Shauna asks about the nature of Leslie and Ben's relationship. Leslie insists it's professional.
jokes.punchline: 'Colleagues with benefits' — Leslie accidentally uses the romantic/sexual phrase, then immediately backpedals.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. 'Colleagues with benefits' is a perfect Freudian slip — it works on multiple levels: as a comedy of embarrassment, as character development (revealing Leslie's feelings), and as a perfectly constructed misdirection. The desperate backpedal ('We're colleagues who benefit from the fact that we're also friends') is even funnier than the slip itself. The structure is nearly perfect: setup, accidental punchline, correction that makes it worse. Extremely quotable and a genuine highlight.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not what RoboCop says. He says 'Dead or alive, you're coming with me.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, he says 'Dead or alive, you're coming with me' in the first film, but in RoboCop 2 and 3 the line is slightly different depending on—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben. Ben, no. I was just trying to make a cool action movie reference to seem impressive. You don't need to correct me.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, if you're going to reference something, you should get it right.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's not the point! The point was to seem cool, not to be accurate about 1980s sci-fi action cinema!

jokes.text: Leslie closes the interview with: 'I'm sorry, Shauna. I think I need to go. But thank you so much, and as always, everything I said is off the record.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just self-destructed in the newspaper interview
jokes.punchline: 'Everything I said is off the record' — the audacity of trying to retroactively declare everything off the record is peak Leslie disaster management
jokes.explanation: The 'as always, everything I said is off the record' button is a perfect closer to the Shauna scene — it reveals Leslie does this regularly, which makes it funnier. Her breezy 'Bye!' makes the desperation worse. Good character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Garbage? This is OshKosh B'Gosh. It's a children's clothing line, but it's very durable.

jokes.text: Andy tries to write a thank-you note to April's grandmother and gets every detail wrong: 'grandfather' vs 'grandmother,' 'woman' vs 'man,' '$500' vs '$5,' 'Mouse Rat CD' when the grandfather is deaf.
jokes.setup: Andy and Tom need to write a thank-you note to April's grandmother/grandfather for a late birthday check.
jokes.punchline: Every single detail Andy writes is wrong: the gender, the amount, the gift — culminating in sending a CD to a deaf person.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully escalating joke. Each correction reveals a new level of Andy's incompetence — wrong gender, wrong amount, wrong gift (a CD for a deaf person) — and the escalation structure is nearly perfect. The CD-for-a-deaf-person is the killer final beat because it's both deeply wrong and completely Andy. Tom's final 'Do you want me to make those changes, or is it good?' is a pitch-perfect deadpan button. This sequence is one of the episode's highlights — great escalation, high character integration, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm going to photograph 'melancholy.' What does melancholy look like?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: A chair.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A sad chair. Got it.

jokes.text: Tom introduces the 'Haverford Schmooze' — three steps: smile, friendly physical contact, flattery. Example: 'Hey, Perd. Was your dad RoboCop? Because your arms are guns.'
jokes.setup: Tom coaches Ben on how to charm Perd Hapley before the interview.
jokes.punchline: The sample flattery line is completely incoherent: 'Was your dad RoboCop? Because your arms are guns' — Tom thinks this is smooth.
jokes.explanation: Tom's schmooze line is a fantastic joke. 'Was your dad RoboCop? Because your arms are guns' is a brilliantly broken compliment — the RoboCop reference makes no logical sense (RoboCop has a gun arm, not 'gun' arms in the attractive sense), and Tom is completely sincere about its effectiveness. Ben's pedantic correction — 'RoboCop didn't have guns for arms' — is the perfect straight-man response. The joke works on three levels: Tom's confidence, the illogic of the compliment, and Ben's inability to let the logical error go.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, floor. I'm sorry for all the pain I've caused you by standing on you.

jokes.text: Ben's correction of Tom's RoboCop flirting tip: 'RoboCop didn't have guns for arms.' Tom: 'Oh, my God. That's so not the point, you nerd.'
jokes.setup: Tom demonstrates his schmooze line about RoboCop.
jokes.punchline: Ben's pedantic literal-mindedness corrects the wrong element — the fictional accuracy of the compliment rather than the social awkwardness of it.
jokes.explanation: Ben's correction of the RoboCop factual error — instead of the obvious problem with the pickup line — is perfect character comedy. It reveals everything about Ben: he's so trapped in his analytical brain that he can't even process social situations as social situations. Tom's exasperated 'That's so not the point, you nerd' is the ideal button. This is among the episode's best exchanges: two characters perfectly bouncing off each other in a way that's entirely specific to them.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee Citizen
dialogue.line: I want a foot massage from Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy Dwyer
dialogue.line: Okay, let me see your feet.

dialogue.speaker: Pawnee Citizen
dialogue.line: Well, I have this really bad corn on my big toe. It's huge and yellow and kind of looks like a little baby chicken is trying to peck its way out of my foot.

jokes.text: Chris criticizes Ben's suit: 'I've let this go on long enough. I like this suit.' Ben: 'You shouldn't, because it looks like garbage.' Ben: 'Your suit looks more like garbage.' Chris: 'Really?' Ben: 'Yeah.' Chris: 'Because Brooks Brothers Boys doesn't make garbage.'
jokes.setup: Chris decides Ben needs a new suit for his media appearances.
jokes.punchline: 'Brooks Brothers Boys' — Ben is wearing a suit from the children's section of Brooks Brothers.
jokes.explanation: 'Brooks Brothers Boys' is a brilliantly specific and devastating punchline. Ben's indignant 'Your suit looks more like garbage' sets up a counterattack, but Chris's reveal that Ben's suit is from the children's department is a perfect reversal. The specificity of 'Boys' is what makes it — 'children's Brooks Brothers' would be less funny than the actual brand name. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, so there's this new roller coaster at the carnival. But here's the thing – you have to be fat enough to ride it. Like, you need to meet a minimum weight requirement. It's the opposite of every other ride.

jokes.text: Andy interprets 'Encapsulate the spirit of melancholy' by photographing a sad desk, a sad wall, a sad floor. 'Boom. A sad desk. Boom. Sad wall. It's art. Anything is anything. Right on.'
jokes.setup: April's photography class assignment is to 'encapsulate the spirit of melancholy.'
jokes.punchline: Andy's art theory — 'It's art. Anything is anything' — is hilariously reductive but delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: 'It's art. Anything is anything.' is a magnificent piece of Andy philosophy. It sounds like a parody of pretentious art-speak but it's actually Andy's genuine attempt at intellectual engagement. 'Sad desk. Sad wall. Sad floor.' as his melancholy portfolio is both absurd and weirdly charming. The 'Right on' is a perfect button. High character integration because this could only be Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I have something I need to confess. When I was seven years old, I wore my mom's wedding dress to school for show and tell.

jokes.text: Andy apologizes to the floor after stepping on it: 'Sorry for stepping on you, floor.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just photographed the floor as 'sad art.'
jokes.punchline: Andy apologizes to the floor — consistent with his logic of finding melancholy in objects, he now feels empathy for them.
jokes.explanation: Five words, maximum comedy. Andy's apology to the floor is a perfect capper to the art bit — it extends the logic of 'anything is anything' to its natural absurd conclusion: if the floor is sad art, it has feelings, and Andy wouldn't want to hurt it. The economy score is 10 because this is the most efficient possible punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I... I can see them. The birds. They're everywhere. They're watching me.

jokes.text: Ron gives April a foot massage and says: 'That's the stuff.' Tom then asks to be next. Ron obliges. 'I have got a corn so big you could slap butter on it.'
jokes.setup: April's list of things she hates includes getting foot massages — apparently from Ron.
jokes.punchline: Ron Swanson giving foot massages is already inherently funny; Tom asking to be next, and Ron's corn complaint, extends the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Ron Swanson earnestly working a heel is inherently hilarious — his dignity is enormous and the task is undignified. 'Work the heel' is a great line, and Tom immediately asking to be next extends the joke perfectly. 'A corn so big you could slap butter on it' is genuinely funny corn imagery.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: So you're telling me you were alone in the woods at midnight with a shovel?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yes, but I was just burying something!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I mean, it was just a dead body—I mean, a dead animal! A dead animal body!

jokes.text: April discovers Tom has added 'foot massage' to Andy's list of her hated tasks. Tom and April's mutual revelation that they're both getting foot massages from Andy.
jokes.setup: April checks in on the chore list; Tom is with her
jokes.punchline: Tom has added his own foot massage to April's hate list — exploiting Andy's romantic gesture for personal benefit
jokes.explanation: Good payoff for Tom's earlier decision to 'help' Andy. His selfish motivation is confirmed — he added his own foot massage. The moment where both April and Tom are receiving foot massages from Andy simultaneously is implied visual comedy. In character for Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Joan! You look amazing. You're like a less angry Jennifer Aniston.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Less angry? Jennifer Aniston's not angry.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know. That's why I said you're like a less angry version of her. You're angrier than Jennifer Aniston.

jokes.text: Perd Hapley's signature intro: 'The story of our guests today is that they are from the Department of Parks and Recreation.'
jokes.setup: Perd introduces his guests on 'Ya' Heard? with Perd.'
jokes.punchline: 'The story of our guests today is that...' — Perd's distinctive verbal tic of over-explaining obvious statements is immediately funny.
jokes.explanation: Perd Hapley is one of the show's best recurring characters. His verbal tic — stating that there IS a story before stating the story — is a brilliant comedy construct. The character integration score is high because this is entirely Perd-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Will you marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Are you serious?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, I thought you were Heidi Klum.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I'm not Heidi Klum.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, you're married to Seal, right?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: No, that's Heidi Klum.

jokes.text: Tom pitches the plus-sized roller coaster: 'Sweetums is even building a plus-sized roller coaster for some of Pawnee's obese thrill-seekers. "You must be this wide to ride."'
jokes.setup: Tom lists Harvest Fest attractions on Perd's show.
jokes.punchline: 'You must be this wide to ride' — inverting the classic theme park height restriction to target obese riders.
jokes.explanation: 'You must be this wide to ride' is a well-constructed inversion of a cultural touchstone. It works as both a commentary on Pawnee's obesity problem (an ongoing show joke) and as a genuinely witty subversion of the familiar phrase. The economy is excellent — the line says everything in six words.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: When you fish, you don't think about the fish's feelings. The fish doesn't think about your feelings. You both just respect each other, and the best fish have a big, lovable fish heart.

jokes.text: At the Ya' Heard? with Perd debrief, Tom says: 'Let's go to the videotape.' Cut to Ben's breakdown on the Perd show.
jokes.setup: Tom describes the Perd interview as having 'some sticky moments'
jokes.punchline: 'Let's go to the videotape' — a sportscaster phrase applied to a municipal government PR disaster
jokes.explanation: Tom's sportscast language is a nice character touch — everything in his life is a production. Works as a structural device and mild character gag.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: This tastes like dirt.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: It does. But it's nutrient-dense dirt.

jokes.text: Footage from Perd's interview: Ben says 'Look. Who hasn't had gay thoughts? Who?' followed by 'I mean, you know, sometimes, I feel like I might need glasses. Is there a bird in here?'
jokes.setup: Leslie shows Tom the disaster footage from Ben's Perd Hapley interview.
jokes.punchline: Ben apparently blurted out a non-sequitur about 'gay thoughts,' then immediately tried to pivot with a glasses comment, then claimed to see a bird.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's funniest moment. 'Who hasn't had gay thoughts? Who?' is completely random and inexplicable, which makes it perfect cringe comedy — the audience has NO idea how the interview got there. Each pivot ('I might need glasses,' 'Is there a bird in here?') is worse than the last, and the escalation from embarrassing to unhinged is masterfully structured. The fact that we see this as a clip Leslie plays for Tom, without explanation, makes it even funnier. Extremely high quotability and a genuine standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I get it. You want me to respond to every single criticism on social media. But have you seen Pawnee's internet infrastructure? We're still using computers from 2003. I can't even load Twitter without the whole system crashing. So you'll have to forgive me if I'm not exactly racing to engage with every troll on the internet when I can barely send an email without the servers catching fire.

jokes.text: Ben's explanation of the Perd meltdown: 'I was 18 when I was elected mayor. Okay? So, excuse me for that. Cindy Eckert had just turned me down for senior prom. Do you know how that... I should call her. I should. No, I shouldn't. And I'm not going to. And I'm proud of myself for that.'
jokes.setup: Ben explains why he melted down in the Perd interview.
jokes.punchline: His explanation devolves from defensive justification to a live crisis about whether to call Cindy Eckert — revealing his trauma is very much unresolved.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'I was 18' to 'Cindy Eckert turned me down for prom' to a live debate about calling her is a perfect character comedy spiral. 'I should call her. I should. No, I shouldn't. And I'm proud of myself for that.' has beautiful internal rhythm and Ben's self-congratulation for not calling her is both sad and funny. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Who hasn't done something dumb at 18?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I slept with my history teacher.

jokes.text: Leslie's summary of Ben's Perd meltdown: 'And then, he talked about feeling up Cindy Eckert for the first time for about five minutes. And then, the show ended. As did our careers and, probably, Harvest Fest.'
jokes.setup: Leslie recaps what happened on Perd's show after the Cindy Eckert digression.
jokes.punchline: 'He talked about feeling up Cindy Eckert for about five minutes.' Plus: 'As did our careers and, probably, Harvest Fest.'
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Ben spent five minutes on-air discussing his teenage sexual experiences with Cindy Eckert is a perfect off-screen escalation — we didn't see it but we can fully imagine it. Leslie's deadpan 'As did our careers and, probably, Harvest Fest' is a great callback button. The structure is excellent: the punchline lands in two beats.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Perd Hapley, more like Turd Crapley.

jokes.text: Andy's sad photography assignment callback: After the foot massage scene, cut to Andy standing next to a random desk saying: 'Boom. Sadness. That's the one.'
jokes.setup: Andy is completing April's photography assignment.
jokes.punchline: 'Boom. Sadness. That's the one.' — Andy has found what he considers the definitive sad image, with total artistic confidence.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the photography bit with Andy's singular, confident 'Boom. Sadness. That's the one.' is a satisfying payoff. The economy is nearly perfect — three words of art critique. Andy's certainty about finding 'the one' sad desk/wall/floor is consistently funny.

jokes.text: Andy tries to get April's younger sister into his car: 'Are you trying to lure this young lady into your van?' Andy: 'Yeah. But she's being really difficult about it, and it's actually not my van. I stole it from a friend of mine. I technically shouldn't be even driving, because my license is crazy expired.'
jokes.setup: Andy arrives late to pick up April's sister from dance class.
jokes.punchline: When confronted about whether he's 'luring' the girl into his van, Andy confirms it — then escalates to stolen van, expired license.
jokes.explanation: Andy's escalating confession is a brilliant character moment. He not only confirms the suspicious behavior ('Yeah') but volunteers that the van is stolen and his license is expired — each detail worse than the last, delivered with total guilelessness. The escalation is perfectly structured and the punchline is compounded by Andy's complete lack of awareness that he's making things worse. Very high quotability.

jokes.text: When a police officer approaches Andy's van, Andy explains: 'I stole it from a friend of mine. I technically shouldn't be even driving, because my license is crazy expired.'
jokes.setup: A cop sees Andy apparently trying to lure a young girl into a van
jokes.punchline: Andy's attempt to explain the innocent situation while simultaneously volunteering that he stole the van and has an expired license — making everything dramatically worse
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy Dwyer honesty-as-self-destruction. When faced with looking like a predator, Andy's defense is to confirm he stole the van and is driving illegally. His total inability to understand what information helps vs. hurts him is perfect characterization. 'My license is crazy expired' — the word 'crazy' as a modifier for 'expired' is an Andy-specific verbal tic that adds character.

jokes.text: Tom mistakes Joan Callamezzo for Jennifer Aniston: 'Joan? I thought you were Jennifer Aniston filming a movie here.'
jokes.setup: Tom runs into Joan Callamezzo before their Pawnee Today interview.
jokes.punchline: Tom's opener is to pretend he mistook her for Jennifer Aniston — transparently false flattery.
jokes.explanation: Tom's schmooze in action — the Jennifer Aniston line is the Haverford Schmooze being deployed. It's Tom-specific but not particularly original as a joke concept.

jokes.text: Tom proposes marriage to Joan: 'Joan, let's make a pact, okay? If we're both still single in an hour, let's get married.' Joan: 'Tom, I'm already married.' Tom: 'That's right. To Seal.' Joan: 'What?' Tom: 'I confused you with Heidi Klum again.'
jokes.setup: Tom proposes a marriage pact to Joan.
jokes.punchline: Tom 'confuses' Joan with Heidi Klum — claiming he always mistakes her for the supermodel as a bizarre form of flattery.
jokes.explanation: The Heidi Klum pivot is a great Tom Haverford schmooze failure. 'To Seal' as his interpretation of Joan's husband, followed by 'I confused you with Heidi Klum again' is both absurd and perfectly in character — Tom's flattery is so convoluted it becomes its own joke. The 'again' implies this is a habit, which is even funnier.

jokes.text: Joan's intro to Pawnee Today: 'Today's guest is Leslie Knope, who is here to tell us how this year's Harvest Festival is going to bankrupt the city.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is expecting a friendly, soft interview on Pawnee Today.
jokes.punchline: Joan's intro frames the interview as hostile from the start — 'bankrupt the city' — completely undercutting Leslie's planned narrative.
jokes.explanation: Joan's ambush framing is a great joke about local news sensationalism. Leslie was expecting a 'puff piece' from a 'big softie' — the gap between expectation and reality is well-executed.

jokes.text: Leslie's instinct when Joan attacks: 'You know? If you want to ask him questions, let's go for it, huh? Just ask any question about his past or present. Just get it over with. Ben, let's get up here.'
jokes.setup: Joan attacks Ben's record on air and Leslie is trying to defend him.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's solution to the attack on Ben is to throw him directly into the line of fire on live TV.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's crisis instinct to 'just get it over with' by exposing Ben directly is both charming and disastrous. The comedy comes from her genuine belief that transparency is the best strategy, even when the transparent subject has already proven he cannot handle scrutiny. Good character comedy of a character defeating themselves.

jokes.text: Ben attempts to answer a caller's question about the budget and stammers: 'I... For...' Leslie jumps in: 'Just to add to what Ben's stammering about, we aren't going to raise taxes.'
jokes.setup: A caller challenges Ben about taxes. Ben immediately begins to melt down again.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's phrase 'to add to what Ben's stammering about' — she acknowledges the meltdown mid-sentence as if it's normal.
jokes.explanation: 'To add to what Ben's stammering about' is a perfectly casual acknowledgment of disaster. Leslie's ability to normalize and pivot through catastrophe is a great character trait, and the phrasing is both natural-sounding and extremely funny. This is a callback to his earlier meltdowns that escalates the running gag.

jokes.text: Ron gives April fishing advice she didn't ask for, using an extended fish metaphor for Andy: 'When you have a fish on the line, you don't just drag it behind the boat. You either reel it in or you cut him loose. Especially if he's a nice fish with a big, lovable fish heart.'
jokes.setup: April insists she doesn't want fishing advice and doesn't fish.
jokes.punchline: 'A nice fish with a big, lovable fish heart' — Ron's Andy metaphor becomes increasingly sincere and specific in its fishiness.
jokes.explanation: Ron dispensing life wisdom through fishing metaphors is perfect character comedy. But the joke escalates beautifully: 'a nice fish with a big, lovable fish heart' reveals that Ron has internalized Andy's sweetness so completely that he can only express it through the one vocabulary he has. The earnestness of 'lovable fish heart' is the key — Ron genuinely means this as a compliment and it's somehow more touching for being ridiculous.

jokes.text: Chris describes his tea: 'Verosian tea really supercharges the bacteria in your colon. Plus, it smells interesting. Waft it.' Ann: 'Are we actually ever going to drink it, or we're just going to sniff it?' Chris: 'I love sniffing. Don't get me wrong.'
jokes.setup: Chris serves Ann a peculiar tea as they try to have a relationship conversation.
jokes.punchline: 'I love sniffing. Don't get me wrong.' — Chris enthusiastically endorses smelling tea rather than drinking it, completely derailing the conversation.
jokes.explanation: Chris's wellness enthusiasm as romantic obstacle is consistently funny. 'I love sniffing. Don't get me wrong' is a slightly odd phrasing that's funnier than a straightforward version would be. The 'supercharges the bacteria in your colon' opener is appropriately disgusting for a romance scene.

jokes.text: Chris describes his next assignment: 'A town called Snerling, Indiana. The cows outnumber the people forty to one.' Ann: 'It sounds amazing.'
jokes.setup: Chris explains where he's going next after Indianapolis.
jokes.punchline: Ann's sincere 'It sounds amazing' about a tiny Indiana town where cows outnumber humans 40-to-1.
jokes.explanation: Ann's enthusiasm for an obviously undesirable posting is mildly funny. The '40 to 1' cow-to-human ratio is a good specific detail. A solid but unremarkable moment.

jokes.text: Chris and Ann try to drink the colon-bacteria tea: 'Wow, that's disgusting.' Chris: 'Yes, it's very hard to drink.'
jokes.setup: After all the build-up about the virtuous tea, they finally drink it.
jokes.punchline: It's disgusting. Chris cheerfully confirms this as if it's a feature, not a bug.
jokes.explanation: A good callback payoff — the disgusting tea that Chris promoted as wonderful. 'It's very hard to drink' delivered with Chris's relentless positivity is a solid character beat. Not exceptional but well-placed.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Okay. First of all, why does everyone in this town use AltaVista? Is it 1997?'
jokes.setup: A caller mentions looking Ben up on AltaVista.
jokes.punchline: 'Why does everyone in this town use AltaVista? Is it 1997?' — Ben's outsider perspective on Pawnee's technological backwardness.
jokes.explanation: The payoff on the AltaVista running gag is well-timed. 'Is it 1997?' is a sharp, economical observation and Ben finally getting a coherent, confident moment in his on-air disaster is a satisfying character beat. The callback structure earns bonus points.

jokes.text: Ben's redemption moment: 'And yeah, I screwed up when I was 18, but who doesn't do dumb stuff when they're 18?' Joan: 'I stole my gym teacher's husband.'
jokes.setup: Ben makes a relatable appeal about youthful mistakes.
jokes.punchline: Joan's overshare — 'I stole my gym teacher's husband' — as her equivalent youthful mistake completely derails the moment.
jokes.explanation: Joan's confession is magnificent. Ben builds to a genuine, almost touching moment of vulnerability — and Joan's response is so specific, so dark, and so Joan that it completely takes over the scene. 'I stole my gym teacher's husband' is a perfect non-sequitur that's both character-defining and hilarious. The specificity (not just 'a husband' but 'my gym teacher's') elevates it significantly. This is the episode's climax and one of its very best jokes.

jokes.text: After Joan's admission, Ben and Leslie exchange a look, and Ben says 'So, there you go.' Leslie: 'Well. What else you got, callers?'
jokes.setup: Joan has just confessed to stealing her gym teacher's husband, derailing the interview.
jokes.punchline: The wordless exchange between Ben and Leslie — two people who realize they've accidentally won by making the interviewer confess her own scandal.
jokes.explanation: 'Well. What else you got, callers?' is perfect Leslie Knope energy — she pivots instantly from disaster to triumph. 'So, there you go' from Ben is a great deadpan button. The reaction beat of two characters realizing they've accidentally turned the tables is satisfying.

jokes.text: The final caller on Pawnee Today asks: 'Yeah, hi. Can you tell me more about the corn maze at the Harvest Festival? Are dogs allowed?'
jokes.setup: After the dramatic climax of Joan's confession, the show takes another caller.
jokes.punchline: The caller wants to know about dogs at the corn maze — a completely mundane question after an absolutely chaotic interview.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of intense drama followed by a completely mundane 'are dogs allowed?' is excellent comedy of bathos. It also works as a commentary on local news — all that drama, and a citizen just wants to know about dog policy. The beat after the question (the implied pause of Leslie's response) adds to the joke.

jokes.text: April's condition for Andy: 'I better be the only person you kissed today.' Andy: 'Yeah, I'm positive that you are.'
jokes.setup: April tentatively agrees to let Andy continue doing her tasks.
jokes.punchline: April's romantic possessiveness is expressed as a threat, and Andy's response — genuinely confident he hasn't kissed anyone else — is both sweet and funny.
jokes.explanation: A sweet character beat that's funny because of the context — we've just seen Andy accidentally implicate himself in car theft and driving without a license. 'Yeah, I'm positive' is gently funny because of its earnestness.

jokes.text: Leslie's dinner with Perd: Leslie claims something is a birthmark and a childhood scar while Perd stares at it: 'I can't look away. It's amazing.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is having dinner with Perd to do damage control.
jokes.punchline: Perd is staring at something on Leslie's face/body that she insists is a birthmark and a scar — but Perd cannot look away from whatever it actually is.
jokes.explanation: This is a visual gag that plays better on screen. The audience can presumably see what Perd is looking at, but Leslie's increasingly specific denials ('This is a birthmark. This is a scar from when I was nine') while Perd says 'I can't look away. It's amazing' creates good cringe discomfort. Perd's signature deadpan sincerity makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Tom says about Perd's show: 'More like "Turd Crapley."' Then: 'Yes. Yes. Yeah? Bravo! Thank you very much.'
jokes.setup: Perd signs off with 'I'm Perd Hapley, Channel Four.'
jokes.punchline: 'Turd Crapley' — Tom's childish pun on Perd's name, followed by him applauding his own joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Turd Crapley' is juvenile potty humor but Tom's self-congratulation — 'Yes. Yes. Bravo! Thank you very much' — saves it. The joke is really about Tom's enormous ego more than the pun itself. Character-specific and gets a mild laugh.

tmdb_overview: While advertising for the Harvest Festival, Ben has to deal with some troubling questions about his past. Meanwhile, Andy continues to try to win April back.
insight: Media blitz strategy backfires into 53 jokes across high-cringe character moments.
